Volume 12 · Chapter 07

Difference-in-differences and event studies

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v12-c06

By the endDefend counterfactual trends and handle treatment timing and heterogeneous effects.

Volume 12 · Chapter 7

Difference-in-differences and event studies

A policy begins in one region while another remains untreated. Comparing their changes removes a fixed level difference, but it does not reveal the treated region's missing counterfactual change. With many adoption dates, a regression can also subtract the evolving effect in an already-treated region. This chapter separates the causal target, the counterfactual restriction, the regression's algebra and the source of sampling uncertainty.

Capability. Derive conditional and group-time difference-in-differences (DID), account for finite-cell nuisance estimation, audit the weights and leads of a fully specified staggered-adoption regression, choose anticipation-safe comparisons, and construct sharp sensitivity bounds and an explicitly justified confidence projection. Six original finite cases supply exact evidence. They are not empirical policy estimates.

Prerequisites. Chapter 1 supplies iid laws, multivariate central limits and delta methods; Chapter 2 supplies partial regression; Chapter 3 distinguishes moment restrictions and identification; Chapter 5 supplies whole-unit sampling and finite-cell influence arguments; Chapter 6 supplies potential outcomes and the distinction between an assignment law and a sampling law. Independent sampling of units does not mean that policy adoption was randomized.

1. The missing trend is the identifying restriction

Use a stable population of units observed on a fixed calendar. G is the first treatment date; G=∞ denotes a genuinely never-treated unit. Treatment is absorbing, Dₜ=1{t≥G}. Let Yₜ(g) be the potential outcome at date t under first adoption at g, and Yₜ(∞) the untreated potential outcome. Impose consistency Yₜ=Yₜ(G) and no interference across units; adoption reversals, spillovers, selective panel loss and changing measurements require different models. For a treated cohort g and t≥g, define ATT(g,t)=E[Yₜ(g)−Yₜ(∞)|G=g]. Outcomes and their differences have the same outcome units.

First assume no anticipation: Yₛ(g)=Yₛ(∞) for s<g. For a clean baseline b<g and a comparison event C whose members are untreated and unaffected at both b and t, add and subtract the treated cohort's untreated change:

E[Yₜ−Y_b|G=g]−E[Yₜ−Y_b|C]
=ATT(g,t)+E[Yₜ(∞)−Y_b(∞)|G=g]−E[Yₜ(∞)−Y_b(∞)|C].

The equality is an accounting identity for potential-outcome means. Parallel trends sets its last difference to zero. It concerns the unobserved change the treated cohort would have experienced, not equality of observed levels or random adoption. Equality of earlier observed trends can refute some stories when violated, but cannot prove this future counterfactual equality. A zero or insignificant lead is neither a design theorem nor a causal guarantee.

Conditional identification. Let H be a finite-valued baseline covariate, measured before anticipation can affect it. For every cell represented in cohort g require a positive eligible comparison probability and

E[Yₜ(∞)−Y_b(∞)|G=g,H=h]=E[Yₜ(∞)−Y_b(∞)|C,H=h].

Apply the previous identity within each cell, then average with P(H=h|G=g), the treated cohort's distribution. Averaging instead over comparison frequencies generally changes the target. Predetermined measurement of H does not establish the displayed restriction; it only avoids one way that treatment could alter the conditioning variable. The scoped Callaway–Sant'Anna December 2020 manuscript motivates these group-time and conditional targets. The finite-cell proof and inference below use their own stated sampling law.

2. Conditional DID, odds weights and the estimated-cell influence

For this section use a two-group population: A=1 denotes the target treated group and A=0 its clean comparison group. We observe N iid complete unit records (A,H,ΔY), where ΔY=Yₜ−Y_b; dependence between dates within a unit is allowed. H has finitely many cells with positive probabilities, ε≤p(h)=P(A=1|H=h)≤1−ε for some ε>0, and E[(ΔY)²]<∞. Let π=P(A=1), mₐ(h)=E[ΔY|A=a,H=h] and d(h)=m₁(h)−m₀(h). Under the preceding consistency, baseline and conditional-trend assumptions, τ=ATT=E[d(H)|A=1]. Without those assumptions this is still an observed-data contrast, but need not be the causal ATT.

Outcome regression and normalized true odds. Conditioning on H gives E[(1−A)p(H)/(1−p(H))]=E[p(H)]=π. Similarly, the comparison weighted outcome mean divided by π is E[p(H)m₀(H)]/π=E[m₀(H)|A=1]. Consequently

τ=E[A{ΔY−m₀(H)}]/π
=E[AΔY]/π−E[(1−A)p(H)ΔY/(1−p(H))]/π.

The two weight systems each sum to one in population. Overlap is substantive: an H cell found only among treated units supplies no observed m₀(h). Large odds can also make the variance large even when the expectation is identified.

A population double-robust identity, with its denominator fixed. For finite candidate functions p̃(h) bounded away from 0 and 1 and m̃(h), define

T(p̃,m̃)=π−1E[{A−(1−A)p̃(H)/(1−p̃(H))}{ΔY−m̃(H)}].
T(p̃,m̃)−τ=π−1E[(p(H)−p̃(H)){m₀(H)−m̃(H)}/(1−p̃(H))].

To prove it, condition on H. The numerator's conditional mean is p(m₁−m̃)−(1−p)p̃(m₀−m̃)/(1−p̃). Subtract p(m₁−m₀); factor the remaining term using p−(1−p)p̃/(1−p̃)=(p−p̃)/(1−p̃). Taking expectations proves the remainder. It is zero if either candidate equals its truth. Both terms here use the actual treated share π; separately renormalizing misspecified comparison odds generally changes this exact remainder. This population identity is not a general machine-learning, cross-fitting or high-dimensional inference theorem.

Finite-cell estimator and proof of its influence. Let Nₐₕ be cell/group counts, N₁=∑ₕN₁ₕ and ΔȲₐₕ their outcome-change means. When every group/cell is observed, use

τ̂=∑ₕ(N₁ₕ/N₁)(ΔȲ₁ₕ−ΔȲ₀ₕ).

There are finitely many sample frequencies and outcome sums. Their positive population denominators and finite second moments give a joint iid CLT and a differentiable ratio map. Differentiating the treated frequency weights and their denominator contributes A{d(H)−τ}/π. Differentiating the treated cell mean contributes A{ΔY−m₁(H)}/π. Differentiating the comparison cell mean contributes −(1−A)p(H){ΔY−m₀(H)}/[π(1−p(H))]. Thus

√N(τ̂−τ)=N−1/2∑ᵢφᵢ+op(1),
φ=A{ΔY−m₀(H)−τ}/π−(1−A)p(H){ΔY−m₀(H)}/[π(1−p(H))],
V=E[φ²], so √N(τ̂−τ) ⇒ Normal(0,V).

The influence has mean zero. Its first derivation makes clear that treated-cell composition is estimated, not fixed. Replacing π,p,m₀,τ by their cell estimates in φ and averaging φ̂² consistently estimates V by finite-cell laws for counts, ΔY and (ΔY)². Divide by N for the estimator variance; a positive V is required for normal studentization. A missing group/cell makes the displayed estimate unavailable. Its probability is at most the finite sum of (1−P(A=a,H=h))ᴺ, which tends to zero; an arbitrary fixed value on that exceptional event defines an auxiliary sequence for the limit proof, not an imputation policy. This theorem assumes independent whole units, not arbitrary policy-cluster dependence or many people in a fixed number of policy clusters.

Worked example 1: a covariate changes the appropriate comparison

The four probabilities P(A,H), in order (1,0),(1,1),(0,0),(0,1), are 1/8,3/8,3/8,1/8. An independent fair sign e adds outcome noise. Baseline outcomes are zero; untreated changes are 1+2H+e and treatment effects are 2+2H. Observed changes are ΔY=1+2H+A(2+2H)+e. The eight atoms have their group/cell probability divided equally across e=±1. The model stipulates conditional parallel trends and no anticipation; neither is inferred from the regression.

Here π=1/2, p(0)=1/4, p(1)=3/4, m₀=(1,3), m₁=(3,7), and treated cell frequencies are (1/4,3/4). The ATT is (1/4)2+(3/4)4=7/2. The treated mean change is 6 and the comparison mean is 3/2, so unadjusted DID is 9/2. Different H frequencies create the extra 1; untreated changes are parallel conditional on H, not unconditionally.

The influence's treated composition component has variance 3/2, its treated-noise component has variance 2, and its comparison-noise component has variance 14/3. These components are orthogonal by conditional mean zero and disjoint treatment groups. Therefore V=3/2+2+14/3=49/6. Omitting estimated composition would incorrectly give 20/3 for this estimator. With working p̃=1/2 and m̃=0, the population double-robust functional is 9/2 and the remainder is 1; making either function correct restores 7/2. Calling a formula robust does not protect it when both needed models are wrong.

3. Two-way fixed effects: comparison weights versus effect weights

Consider a finite balanced table with equal weight per group/date cell. Let F contain group and date fixed effects with a nonredundant normalization, and let M_F project off their span. Partial regression gives β̂TWFE=(D′M_FD)⁻¹D′M_FY when D′M_FD>0. For a balanced table, D̃=M_FD is obtained by subtracting its row and column means and adding its grand mean. Since D̃′F=0 and D̃′D=D̃′D̃,

β̂TWFE=∑g,tD̃gtYgt/∑g,tD̃gt².

If untreated cell means are additive a_g+λ_t and there is no anticipation, write Y_gt=a_g+λ_t+D_gtτ_gt. The coefficient is then ∑_{D_gt=1}w_gtτ_gt, where w_gt=D̃_gt/∑D̃². The weights sum to one because ∑D̃D=∑D̃², but a treated cell can have D̃_gt<0. The additive untreated model supplies the causal interpretation; the regression identity holds without it. The scoped Goodman-Bacon August 2020 author manuscript provides the broader comparison decomposition. We prove the complete original finite decomposition below, not its all-design extension.

Worked example 2: positive effects and a negative regression coefficient

Three equally weighted cohorts adopt at dates 2, 4 and ∞, called E, L and N. Untreated potential outcomes are zero at every date. The observed table is:

CohortDate 1Date 2Date 3Date 4
E, adoption 20137
L, adoption 40002
N, never0000

Twelve times the residual treatment table is ((−5,3,3,−1),(1,−3,−3,5),(4,0,0,−4)). Squared residual treatment sums to 5/6. The four treated-cell effect weights, in order (E2,E3,E4,L4), are (3/10,3/10,−1/10,1/2). The coefficient is 3/10+9/10−7/10+1=3/2. Increasing the positive E4 effect from 7 to 23 changes the coefficient to −1/10. The negative result is possible even though every treatment effect is positive.

Four comparisons, exactly. Write Ē₂:₄=(E₂+E₃+E₄)/3, and similarly for any displayed consecutive range. Define C₁=(Ē₂:₄−E₁)−(N̄₂:₄−N₁), C₂=(L₄−L̄₁:₃)−(N₄−N̄₁:₃), C₃=(Ē₂:₃−E₁)−(L̄₂:₃−L₁), and C₄=(L₄−L̄₂:₃)−(E₄−Ē₂:₃). The first two compare adopters with never-treated units; C₃ uses L while it is not yet treated; C₄ uses E after it is already treated.

β̂TWFE=(3/10)C₁+(3/10)C₂+(1/5)C₃+(1/5)C₄.

To prove this for every outcome table with this design, expand its right side in the order (E1,…,E4,L1,…,L4,N1,…,N4). Its coefficient vector is (−1/2,3/10,3/10,−1/10,1/10,−3/10,−3/10,1/2,2/5,0,0,−2/5), exactly D̃/(5/6). In the supplied table the four contrasts are (11/3,2,2,−3), producing 3/2. C₄=2−(7−2)=−3 subtracts the early cohort's effect increase. Positive comparison weights therefore coexist with a negative weight on E4's effect. This is a proved finite identity under the declared equal-cell design, not a claim that every specification has these four weights.

4. A lead coefficient need not be a clean pretrend

An event-study regression replaces the one treatment indicator by indicators for relative time k=t−g among ever-treated groups. Its coefficient meaning depends on all included categories, the omitted category, the support, any binning, and the fixed effects. A zero true pre-treatment effect does not generally force every fitted lead to zero when effects vary across cohorts. The inspected Sun–Abraham September 2020 manuscript discusses this contamination and cohort-specific alternatives. Our regression retains impact k=0 and derives every coefficient explicitly: no anticipation sets true pre-effects to zero only for k<0.

Worked example 3: two artificial leads from a complete table

Use exactly example 2's table. Include three group indicators, date indicators for dates 2, 3, 4, and all observed event indicators except k=−1. The five event columns are k=(−3,−2,0,1,2); never-treated rows have zeros in all five. There are 12 rows and 11 regression columns. Let Z̃ be the event design after removing the group/date effects. Its residual Gram and outcome cross product are

Z̃′Z̃=A/12, Z̃′Y=(7,3,−17,4,28)′/12,
A=((6,−2,−1,1,1),
(−2,6,−5,1,1),
(−1,−5,14,−1,−5),
(1,1,−1,6,−2),
(1,1,−5,−2,6)).

Elimination on A has pivots 6,16/3,17/2,93/17,96/31, giving det(A)=4608 and det(Z̃′Z̃)=1/54. Thus the normalization has full event rank. The following table gives the entire outcome operator O=(Z̃′Z̃)⁻¹Z̃′. Each entry is a four-date vector for the indicated cohort, and every displayed entry is divided by 8:

Event k8O on E1,E2,E3,E48O on L1,L2,L3,L48O on N1,N2,N3,N4
−3(−3,3,0,0)(8,0,−5,−3)(−5,−3,5,3)
−2(−1,1,0,0)(0,8,−7,−1)(1,−9,7,1)
0(−4,4,0,0)(0,0,−4,4)(4,−4,4,−4)
1(−5,−3,8,0)(0,0,−3,3)(5,3,−5,−3)
2(−7,−1,0,8)(0,0,−1,1)(7,1,1,−9)

Multiplying O by the complete outcome table gives coefficients (−3/8,−1/8,3/2,27/8,57/8). In this zero-untreated-outcome case, if a=τ_E2 and b=τ_L4, the leads are 3(a−b)/8 and (a−b)/8; the impact is (a+b)/2; and later coefficients are τ_E3+3(b−a)/8 and τ_E4+(b−a)/8. Here a=1 and b=2. No untreated trend or anticipation exists, yet both fitted leads are nonzero. Changing the late impact to 1 gives coefficients (0,0,1,3,7) under the same design. These formulas are tied to the full displayed design, not transferable to an unspecified set of binned leads and lags.

Clean supported targets. Using the never-treated cohort with each cohort's last unaffected baseline identifies each of (1,3,7,2) directly. Equal weighting among supported cohorts gives impact average (1+2)/2=3/2, while event time 1 has only E and average 3. Their difference is 3/2. A fixed-E target has impact 1 and event-one effect 3, a difference of 2. The comparisons ask different questions because the supported cohort distribution changes. More starkly, if all E post effects were 1 and L's impact remained 2, the changing-composition averages would move from 3/2 to 1 although each cohort's effect is constant; the E-only averages would remain 1 and 1. No unsupported L event-one effect is filled with zero.

Cohort-specific contrasts followed by declared nonnegative weights can target an interpretable supported average. Their validity still requires clean controls, counterfactual trends, observation support and the relevant sampling argument. The finite operator example proves a point-estimation failure; it supplies neither arbitrary cluster inference nor a general simultaneous-band theorem.

5. Anticipation changes both the baseline and eligible controls

Now suppose a known nonnegative integer a bounds anticipation: Yₛ(g)=Yₛ(∞) only for s<g−a. For a post-adoption target t≥g, choose baseline b=g−a−1. A not-yet-treated comparison must have first adoption G>t+a, not merely G>t. This makes both its target date and its earlier baseline unaffected. Require b to be observed and the needed target/comparison probabilities within each covariate cell to be positive. With these conditions the group-time identity in section 1 applies again. A cohort with no observed unaffected baseline, such as an always-treated group, is not identified by this contrast.

At the end of a data window, observing no adoption through T is not the same as knowing G>T+a. If t+a exceeds the observed calendar, a genuinely never-treated comparison or additional known future adoption information is needed. When the last eligible controls disappear, the affected target cells become unsupported; changing their effects to zero would be an assumption, not an estimate.

Worked example 4: the untreated indicator hides an anticipatory response

Calendar dates are 1,2,3,4, a=1, and the target cohort adopts at g=3. Every group's untreated path is (1,2,3,4). The target's observed path is (1,4,8,9), with an anticipatory effect 2 at date 2 and treatment effect 5 at dates 3 and 4. A never-treated group follows the untreated path.

At t=3, using baseline 2 gives (8−4)−(3−2)=3, subtracting the target's own anticipation. The required baseline is b=3−1−1=1, giving (8−1)−(3−1)=5. The date-4 target also equals (9−1)−(4−1)=5 with the never-treated comparison.

Suppose another cohort adopts at 4 and has anticipation effect 2 at date 3, so its date-3 outcome is 5 although D₃=0. Its baseline-1 outcome is 1. Using it at date 3 gives (8−1)−(5−1)=3. It is ineligible because G=4 does not exceed t+a=4. With only these two adopting cohorts and no never-treated group, the date-3 target lacks an eligible control. Its value is not identified by this DID design, despite every realized number being observed.

6. Partial identification from explicit trend restrictions

Use clean population group contrasts, not contaminated raw TWFE leads. Normalize a baseline date 0 and write the reduced-form contrast at each date as bₜ=τₜ+δₜ, where τₜ is the treatment effect and δₜ the untreated treated-minus-comparison trend departure relative to date 0. Let δ₀=b₀=0. No anticipation makes τₜ=0 in preperiods, so their observed population contrasts fix δₜ. Post-treatment data alone cannot separate the two terms.

Why perfect pretrends do not finish identification. Let all observed preperiod group gaps be zero and the observed post gap be 4. One potential-outcome law has untreated post gap 0 and effect 4; another has untreated post gap 3 and effect 1. Both reproduce every observed gap and have no anticipation. Their different counterfactual post paths are precisely what preperiod equality leaves unresolved.

Attainment and sharpness. Fix the observed preperiod coordinates and let K be the allowed set of post departure vectors. If K is nonempty, compact and convex, the image of K under θ=ℓ′(b_post−δ_post) is a closed interval. Continuity on compact K gives attained minimum and maximum; linearity and convexity provide every value between the endpoint images. A restriction that conflicts with the preperiod information gives an empty fiber, not an interval with invented endpoints. Closed convexity without compactness is not by itself an attainment theorem for arbitrary linear images. The examples below parameterize compact squares directly.

To show the bounds are sharp in the unrestricted outcome model, for every allowed δ set comparison outcomes to zero, treated untreated means to δ at each date, and treated post-treatment outcomes to the observed b. Set the post treatment effects to b−δ and use the fixed observed preperiod path with zero pre-effects. This constructs the specified observed contrasts for every feasible departure path under consistency and no interference. No extra outcome bounds or treatment-effect sign restriction is being imposed.

Worked example 5: two different meanings of a tolerable trend departure

Use unit-spaced periods. Preperiod departures at dates −2,−1,0 are (−2,−1,0); post reduced forms at dates 1,2 are (4,6). The target is θ=(τ₁+τ₂)/2. Preperiod increments are both 1.

Relative increment restriction. For a dimensionless M̄≥0, require each post increment's absolute size to be at most M̄ times the largest observed preperiod increment, here 1. Let u=δ₁−δ₀ and v=δ₂−δ₁; then (u,v)∈[−M̄,M̄]², δ₁=u and δ₂=u+v. Therefore θ=5−u−v/2 and

Θrelative=[5−3M̄/2,5+3M̄/2].

The four square vertices give targets 5−3M̄/2,5−M̄/2,5+M̄/2,5+3M̄/2. At M̄=1 the interval is [7/2,13/2]. At M̄=0 post departures are constant at zero, giving θ=5. This restriction bounds post increments relative to past increments; it does not require the post increment to remain near the previous value 1.

Smoothness restriction. Instead require |δ₁−2δ₀+δ₋₁|≤M and |δ₂−2δ₁+δ₀|≤M, with M≥0 in outcome units per squared period. Write the post increments as 1+e₀ and 1+e₀+e₁, where |e₀|,|e₁|≤M. Thus δ₁=1+e₀, δ₂=2+2e₀+e₁ and θ=7/2−3e₀/2−e₁/2. The sharp interval is

Θsmooth=[7/2−2M,7/2+2M].

The four vertices give 7/2−2M,7/2−M,7/2+M,7/2+2M. At M=1 the interval is [3/2,11/2]. At M=0 the differential trend continues linearly with departures 1 and 2, giving θ=7/2, not 5. Zero curvature is not a parallel-trends assumption. Both sets are compact convex images and the preceding construction proves sharpness. They are population identification intervals, not confidence intervals.

The inspected Rambachan–Roth published paper develops structured sensitivity and inference. We distinguish its two restriction families, provide original finite sharpness proofs, and next prove a limited confidence construction rather than invoke its uninspected general inference results.

7. Sampling uncertainty includes uncertainty about the preperiod

For a separate explicit experiment, suppose (b̂_pre,b̂_post) is exactly bivariate Gaussian with means (b_pre,b_post) and known marginal standard deviations σ_pre,σ_post>0. Correlation may be arbitrary. This is a stipulated finite sampling law, not an automatic consequence of a DID estimator or a fixed count of policy clusters. Let z=Φ⁻¹(1−α/4), 0<α<1, and C be the rectangle b_j∈[b̂_j−zσ_j,b̂_j+zσ_j]. Each coordinate interval fails with probability α/2; the union bound gives P(b∈C)≥1−α without independence.

Normalize the departure at a baseline to zero, assume no pre-effect, and impose |δ_post|≤M̄|b_pre|. For every b∈C collect all allowed δ_post and all θ=b_post−δ_post. The compatible triples form a nonempty compact set: δ_post=0 is always allowed, the constraint is closed, and |δ_post| is bounded by M̄ times the largest |b_pre| in the compact rectangle. This joint set need not be convex; the example below proves its projected interval by explicit witnesses. On the event b_true∈C the actual admissible pair (b_true,δ_true) is included, so this projection contains θ_true. That proves finite coverage at least 1−α for every mean and departure satisfying this exact Gaussian model and restriction. A plug-in identified interval computed only at b̂ has no such proof.

Worked example 6: a zero estimated pretrend still has uncertainty

Observe (b̂_pre,b̂_post)=(0,4), let σ_pre=σ_post=1/5, α=0.05 and M̄=1. Write h=Φ⁻¹(0.9875)/5. Then b_pre∈[−h,h], b_post∈[4−h,4+h], and allowed departures satisfy |δ_post|≤|b_pre|≤h. The smallest effect is 4−h−h and the largest is 4+h+h. They are attained by taking |b_pre|=h, the appropriate post endpoint, and the opposite effect-producing departure endpoint. Fixing b_pre=h and varying b_post and δ_post fills every value between them. Therefore the complete projected confidence interval is

[4−2h,4+2h], h=Φ⁻¹(0.9875)/5≈0.448280545521,
approximately [3.103438908958,4.896561091042].

The symbolic interval defines the coverage statement; rounded endpoints are numerical illustrations. More generally, with these observed estimates and equal halfwidth h, the interval is [4−(1+M̄)h,4+(1+M̄)h]. At M̄=0 only post-mean uncertainty remains; at M̄=2 it is approximately [2.655158363437,5.344841636563]. Treating the estimate b̂_pre=0 as a known population zero would wrongly discard preperiod uncertainty. This directly proved projection is not the general uniform asymptotic, bootstrap or conditional-testing procedure in the sensitivity literature.

8. Derive, diagnose and transfer

  1. Starting from the potential outcomes, derive the group-time DID identity in section 1. State the precise role of consistency, interference, an unaffected baseline and parallel trends. How do the baseline and control eligibility change with a known anticipation horizon a?
  2. For example 1, derive every group/cell probability, p(H), treated covariate frequency, conditional change mean, ATT and unadjusted DID. Prove the true normalized-odds identity and compute its comparison counterfactual mean.
  3. Derive the exact population remainder for T(p̃,m̃). Evaluate all four combinations of p̃=p or 1/2 and m̃=m₀ or 0 in example 1. Explain why arbitrarily renormalizing misspecified comparison odds is not covered by the displayed remainder.
  4. Differentiate the finite-cell estimator in section 2 to derive its influence. Compute each of the three orthogonal variance components in example 1 and their total. State the exceptional finite-sample event and the normalization for the estimator's covariance.
  5. Reconstruct example 2's residual treatment table, squared norm and all four effect weights. Replace E4's effect by x>0 and solve exactly for the zero and negative TWFE boundaries. Explain why the effect weights sum to one without all being positive.
  6. Define the four two-by-two comparisons in example 2 and evaluate them. Prove their weighted sum equals TWFE for every outcome table with this fixed design by matching all twelve cell coefficients. Identify the changing treatment effect subtracted by the fourth comparison.
  7. Use the full event design in example 3 to verify its residual Gram rank and solve for all five coefficients. Express each coefficient in terms of the four treated-cell effects when untreated outcomes are zero. Recompute the vector when L4 changes from 2 to 1.
  8. For example 3 compare changing-cohort and fixed-E impact/event-one targets. Then change all three E post effects to 1 while retaining L4=2. Show a changing aggregate despite constant cohort effects, and explain why the missing L event-one effect is not zero.
  9. In example 4 calculate the date-3 estimates using baseline 2, the correct baseline 1 and the anticipatory adoption-4 comparison. Explain the absence of identification when no eligible controls remain, and the additional information needed when t+a exceeds the observed calendar.
  10. Derive both sharp intervals in example 5 by displaying the four vertices and constructing compatible potential outcomes. Evaluate both at bound 1/2 and at zero. Explain the different units and why zero smoothness does not mean parallel trends.
  11. Prove the finite known-Gaussian confidence projection's coverage, accounting for both coordinates. Derive the attained interval for observed (0,4) at M̄=1 and at M̄=2. Contrast this with treating the estimated preperiod mean as an exactly known population zero.
  12. A report pools regions with staggered adoption, bins several leads, sees an insignificant joint lead test, uses all not-yet-adopted regions despite a documented one-period anticipation window, and interprets its TWFE coefficient as an equally weighted ATT. It chooses a sensitivity bound after seeing the estimate and labels a plug-in identified interval a 95% confidence interval. Give six distinct objections, two feasible repairs with explicit remaining assumptions, and a defensible conclusion. The solution rubric allocates 12 points.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Consistency substitutes Y_t(g) for the target's observed outcome and Y_t(∞) for unaffected controls. No interference lets these outcomes be indexed by the unit's own adoption schedule. At an unaffected baseline, target Y_b(g)=Y_b(∞). Add and subtract E[Y_t(∞)|G=g] to get ATT plus the target-minus-control untreated change difference. Parallel trends sets only that final difference to zero; neither equal levels nor random sampling does so. With anticipation a, require b=g−a−1 in the observed calendar and control G>t+a, plus positive target/control support in any conditioning cells. Merely having D_t=0 is insufficient.

  2. P(H=0)=P(H=1)=1/2 and P(A=1)=1/2. Bayes gives p=(1/4,3/4), while P(H|A=1)=(1/4,3/4) and P(H|A=0)=(3/4,1/4). Conditional means are m₀=(1,3), m₁=(3,7), so effects (2,4) yield ATT 7/2. Mean changes are 6 and 3/2; unadjusted DID is 9/2. The unnormalized comparison odds masses are (3/8)(1/3)=1/8 and (1/8)3=3/8, summing to π=1/2. Their normalized mean m₀ is [(1/8)1+(3/8)3]/(1/2)=5/2, so 6−5/2=7/2. In general conditional expectation gives E[(1−A)p/(1−p)f(H)]=E[p f(H)]=E[A f(H)], proving the normalization and the covariate reweighting.

  3. Condition on H and subtract p(m₁−m₀) from p(m₁−m̃)−(1−p)p̃(m₀−m̃)/(1−p̃). The result is (p−p̃)(m₀−m̃)/(1−p̃). Dividing its expectation by π proves the remainder. With both functions correct, with only p correct, or with only m₀ correct, T=7/2. With p̃=1/2 and m̃=0, the remainder is [(1/2)(−1/2)1+(1/2)(1/2)3]/(1/2)=1, giving 9/2. The proof uses the same actual π for both terms. Dividing the second term by its own misspecified expected odds mass changes the functional and its algebra; it needs a different remainder calculation.

  4. The derivative of treated composition contributes A(d−τ)/π; treated means contribute A(ΔY−m₁)/π; controls contribute −(1−A)p(ΔY−m₀)/[π(1−p)]. Their sum is the displayed φ. In the original law, Var(d|A=1)=(1/4)(−3/2)²+(3/4)(1/2)²=3/4, so composition variance is (3/4)/π=3/2. Treated noise contributes 1/π=2. Comparison noise contributes 4[(3/8)(1/3)²+(1/8)3²]=14/3. Conditional noise means and disjoint group indicators make the cross terms zero, giving V=49/6. Omitting composition leaves 20/3, a different variance. Any N_ah=0 makes the finite estimate unavailable; positive cell probabilities make that event vanish for the asymptotic sequence. The estimate's variance is V/N, and normal studentization additionally needs V>0.

  5. Treatment rows are (0,1,1,1),(0,0,0,1),(0,0,0,0); row means are 3/4,1/4,0, date means are 0,1/3,1/3,2/3, and grand mean is 1/3. Subtracting row/date means and adding the grand mean produces the displayed residual table divided by 12. Its squared norm is 120/144=5/6. Dividing treated entries by 5/6 gives (3/10,3/10,−1/10,1/2). The coefficient with E4=x is (22−x)/10, zero at x=22 and negative for x>22; at x=23 it is −1/10. The sum-one identity is D̃′D/D̃′D̃=1. Projection orthogonality guarantees that identity, not positivity of every residual treated entry.

  6. The four contrasts use E versus N on baseline1/post2–4; L versus N on pre1–3/post4; E versus not-yet-L on baseline1/post2–3; and L versus already-E on pre2–3/post4. They are 11/3,2,2,−3. With weights 3/10,3/10,1/5,1/5 their sum is 11/10+3/5+2/5−3/5=3/2. Expanding cell coefficients gives (−1/2,3/10,3/10,−1/10,1/10,−3/10,−3/10,1/2,2/5,0,0,−2/5), the FWL operator on every table. C₄ subtracts the early effect's change 7−(1+3)/2=5 from the late effect 2, so positive comparison weights do not make it a clean late-cohort effect.

  7. The exact Gram is A/12. Its elimination pivots are 6,16/3,17/2,93/17,96/31; their product is 4608, so det(A/12)=1/54>0. Solving Aγ=(7,3,−17,4,28)′ gives γ=(−3/8,−1/8,3/2,27/8,57/8). With a=τ_E2, b=τ_L4, c=τ_E3 and d=τ_E4, applying the displayed full operator gives (3(a−b)/8,(a−b)/8,(a+b)/2,c+3(b−a)/8,d+(b−a)/8). Setting a=b=1,c=3,d=7 gives (0,0,1,3,7). The earlier nonzero leads came from effect heterogeneity in this design, despite zero true pre-effects and untreated trends.

  8. Changing-cohort impact/event-one targets are 3/2 and 3, a difference of 3/2. Fixed E gives 1 and 3, a difference of 2. When E's effects are instead all 1, the changing averages are 3/2 and 1, a difference of −1/2, while fixed-E averages are 1 and 1, difference 0. The late cohort's event-one date is beyond the observed table. It is not an observed zero or a member of the supported event-one average. A fixed-cohort comparison prevents composition from changing, but needs support for that cohort over every compared horizon.

  9. Baseline 2 gives (8−4)−(3−2)=3; baseline 1 with never-treated controls gives (8−1)−(3−1)=5. Adoption-4 controls already have date-3 outcome 5, so the same baseline gives (8−1)−(5−1)=3. Their G=4 fails G>3+1. With no never-treated group and no later eligible cohort, the target cell is unsupported by this identification argument, not zero. If t+a>T, observing no adoption through T cannot rule out an anticipatory response at t; known later adoption status or genuinely never-treated controls are needed.

  10. For relative bounds, departure increments (u,v) lie in the square with vertices (±M̄,±M̄); the four objective values are 5±3M̄/2 and 5±M̄/2. Thus at M̄=1/2 the interval is [17/4,23/4], and at zero it is {5}. For smoothness, the two curvature deviations (e₀,e₁) lie in (±M,±M); the four values are 7/2±2M and 7/2±M. At M=1/2 the interval is [5/2,9/2], and at zero it is {7/2}. All values in each interval follow from convex combinations of vertex departure paths. Set control outcomes zero, target untreated means equal to each departure path, and observed target post means to (4,6); treatment effects fill the difference. This supplies sharp compatible laws. M̄ is a ratio to preperiod increment magnitude; M bounds a second difference in outcome units per squared period. At M=0 the prior unit differential slope continues, so untreated post departures are 1 and 2, not zero.

  11. Each marginal known-normal interval with z=Φ⁻¹(1−α/4) misses with probability α/2. The union bound controls either failure by α, regardless of correlation. Whenever both true means lie in the rectangle, the true allowed departure and target lie in the projected set. At observed (0,4), |b_pre|≤h and b_post∈[4−h,4+h]. With M̄=1, choosing b_pre=h and δ_post∈[−h,h] gives the entire interval [4−2h,4+2h], including both endpoints. With M̄=2 use δ_post∈[−2h,2h], giving [4−3h,4+3h]. Numerically these are approximately [3.103438908958,4.896561091042] and [2.655158363437,5.344841636563]. An estimated premean zero is not a known true zero. If the latter were an additional valid restriction, δ_post would be zero and only [4−h,4+h] post uncertainty would remain; that is a different information contract.

  12. Six distinctions, one point each. (1) A nonrejected observed lead test does not establish the untreated future parallel trend; its power and selection matter. (2) Heterogeneous effects can contaminate leads, and binning/normalization change their operator. (3) TWFE generally has design-dependent effect weights, potentially negative, rather than the claimed equal ATT weights. (4) Not-yet-adopted controls can be anticipating; with a=1, eligibility is G>t+1 and baseline g−2, with supported observation dates. (5) A sensitivity restriction chosen after seeing the result is not independent scientific support for its magnitude and must be disclosed and examined across defensible values. (6) A plug-in population identified interval is not a 95% confidence procedure; both pre and post sampling uncertainty and the actual independent information units require an inferential argument.

    Two repairs, two points each. One repair is to state the target cohorts/horizons, use unaffected baselines and eligible controls, estimate supported cohort-specific contrasts, and aggregate with fixed declared nonnegative weights. This still assumes the relevant counterfactual trends, consistency/no interference and observation support. Another is to justify a range of trend departures from substantive knowledge and report identification bounds separately from a confidence method whose sampling assumptions can be defended. The finite known-Gaussian example cannot simply be asserted for dependent regional estimates; the actual law or a separately justified approximation must be supplied. Other repairs receive credit when their required evidence and remaining limitations are explicit.

    Conclusion, two points. The current regression documents a particular weighted association among the observed adoption paths. Its reported equal-weight causal effect and 95% sensitivity claim have not been established. A defensible report gives the exact target/design and separates missing-counterfactual assumptions from estimation uncertainty, without pretending that a preferred estimator or a passing pretest verifies them.

9. Teach-back and delayed retrieval

Teach-back. Explain to a policy team why positive two-by-two weights need not imply positive treatment-effect weights, and why perfect observed pretrends do not identify the post effect. Use the chapter's numerical counterexamples.

Answer criteria

The late-versus-already-early comparison subtracts the early cohort's changing effect. In the original table it is −3; the positive weight 1/5 on that comparison still contributes a negative E4 effect weight −1/10. Separately, zero preperiod gaps and post gap 4 fit both untreated post gap 0/effect 4 and untreated post gap 3/effect 1. The team should hear which missing counterfactual assumption distinguishes those worlds, not that regression or pretesting supplies it automatically.

Delayed retention. (a) With a=1, g=3 and t=3, what baseline and control-adoption boundary are required? (b) At what E4 effect does the fixed TWFE design cross zero? (c) What are the relative and smoothness identified intervals at bound 1/2? (d) Why does the Gaussian sensitivity projection use both coordinate uncertainties?

Retention answers

(a) Baseline b=1 and controls G>4. (b) E4=22 gives zero; larger values give a negative coefficient. (c) Relative [17/4,23/4], smoothness [5/2,9/2], under their different restrictions. (d) The preperiod population mean determines the allowed departure magnitude and is itself estimated. Covering only the post mean omits that uncertainty; the simultaneous rectangle plus projection has the stated finite coverage proof.

10. Reproduce the finite evidence and keep the scope honest

Run python3 scripts/check_v12_c07.py in the source tree. The standard-library checker is silent on success and its importable check() returns a strict-JSON-compatible summary. It reconstructs the finite joint law, influences, all twelve regression rows, effect/comparison operators, complete event Gram and operator, anticipation comparisons, sensitivity vertices and known-Gaussian calculation. The four-file source package also runs from an unrelated working directory under ordinary or optimized Python without network or shared-library inputs.

The source record reuses four scoped primary inspections with exact versions: the December 2020 Callaway–Sant'Anna and September 2020 Sun–Abraham author-deposited manuscripts, the August 2020 Goodman-Bacon author manuscript, and the published 2023 Rambachan–Roth paper. Selected substantive sections and equation pages were inspected during source preparation, not every appendix or empirical application. Numerical verification does not prove counterfactual assumptions, independence, general uniform inference or external validity. General repeated-cross-section, high-dimensional nuisance, all-design decomposition, multiplier-bootstrap, interactive-dependence and optimized sensitivity-inference results remain beyond the proofs here.

The next chapter, regression discontinuity and synthetic controls, changes the source of the counterfactual comparison. The same discipline remains: specify the target, support, identifying restriction and actual probability law before choosing an estimator.

Sources and further study

  • Difference-in-Differences with Multiple Time Periods — Group-time ATT, conditional trends, overlap, anticipation-safe baselines and controls, and supported cohort aggregation. The chapter proves its finite-cell identification/remainder/influence results directly.
  • Estimating Dynamic Treatment Effects in Event Studies with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects — Contamination of relative-time coefficients under heterogeneity and cohort-specific aggregation. The full original rational regression is independently derived; impact time zero is included explicitly.
  • Difference-in-Differences with Variation in Treatment Timing — Comparison versus treatment-effect weighting in a basic balanced absorbing-treatment TWFE regression. The chapter proves only its complete original three-cohort/four-date decomposition, not the general appendix theorem.
  • A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends — Reduced-form/departure decomposition, relative-increment versus curvature sensitivity, and the difference between identified and confidence sets. Compact fibers and original square sharpness are proved directly, as is a separate finite known-Gaussian projection.
